Charcoal is perfect—smoky flavor and you can easily manage a two-zone setup. Here’s a make-ahead lineup that keeps you social:

- **Potato salad**: Toss cubed red potatoes in mayo, diced pickle, and chives the night before. Keeps chilled, just fluff before serving.  
- **Coleslaw**: Mix shredded cabbage, carrot, and a creamy dressing; refrigerate overnight so flavors meld.  
- **Corn on the cob**: Butter and salt kernels ahead, wrap in foil, and drop them on the grill alongside burgers—takes only 12–15 minutes.  
- **Watermelon cubes**: Cut into bite-sized pieces, add a pinch of salt, store in a container; grab-and-go snack.

Avoid marble entirely—understood. For a high-traffic family bathroom, go with an epoxy grout rather than cement-based grout. Epoxy is nearly non-porous, so it resists water, soap scum, and even harsh cleaners without needing a sealer. If you’ve already chosen cement grout, pick an unsanded formula and use a penetrating sealer rated for wet areas; re-seal every 12–18 months. Keep joints 1/8" wide or less to reduce grout surface area and make maintenance easier.

Marble is indeed costly and maintenance-heavy, so avoiding it is a smart budget move. For your bathroom floor, epoxy grout is the top choice for high-moisture areas since it’s nearly impervious to water, resists mold growth, and won’t stain. It’s more expensive and harder to remove than cement-based grout, but the long-term durability pays off. If you want a middle ground, polymer-modified cement grout with a sealer works, though it’ll need resealing periodically. Skip the couscous entirely—roasted cauliflower rice is a smart swap. Break the cauliflower into small florets, toss with olive oil, salt, pepper, and a pinch of cumin, then spread it on a baking sheet and roast at 400 °F for 20–25 minutes until the edges brown. It soaks up the chicken pan juices just like couscous would, but it’s naturally gluten-free and adds a satisfying nutty crunch to the plate.

A slick way to stretch those drippings is a cornstarch slurry—two teaspoons cornstarch whisked into four tablespoons cold water, then stirred into the pan juices until thickened; cornstarch is both gluten-free and dairy-free. If you want extra depth, add a splash of vegetable stock and a quick pinch of smoked paprika for roasted flavor.

Another safe route is a quick roux made with rice flour—heat one tablespoon rice flour in the pan drippings for sixty seconds, whisk in a half-cup of stock, simmer two minutes. Rice flour thickens smoothly and keeps the gravy light enough for your daughter’s needs.

Skip the shellfish entirely and go strong on vegetables that grill beautifully. Portobello mushrooms tossed in olive oil, garlic, and a splash of balsamic turn into smoky little steaks. Corn on the cob brushed with lime-butter gets caramelized char in about ten minutes. Squash rounds halved lengthwise, drizzled with cumin and chili powder, caramelize nicely. For a protein boost, seasoned tofu cubes on skewers with a sweet soy glaze stay juicy and firm. Add grilled zucchini spears and asparagus for color and crunch.

These options will hold their flavor, won’t cross-contaminate, and give everyone plenty of variety to pick from.

Skip any shellfish-based sides entirely. Instead, bake a big batch of baked beans with a touch of maple and chili; they hold up well in warm weather and don’t need reheating. Add a three-bean salad—kidney, garbanzo, and black beans—tossed in a light vinaigrette, which stays fresh for hours. For crunch and color, set out cucumber-tomato salad chilled in a cooler, plus a tray of carrot sticks with ranch. These options are allergy-safe, easy to prep ahead, and won’t spoil even if the kitchen’s hot.

Skip the ribs and go with sides that travel well and need just a quick toss before serving. A cucumber-tomato salad with red onion and olive oil keeps cool and stays crisp in the fridge until five minutes before kickoff. A herbed potato salad with celery and green onion can be made a day ahead and stays tasty at room temp. For something crunchy and colorful, pair a bag of baby carrots with a batch of quick ranch or yogurt dip. If you want a slightly sweeter element, a slow-cooker corn salsa with lime and cilantro reheats fast and feels festive. All of these require minimal setup, pack in containers, and can be left on a side table without spoiling.

The thermal conductivity is also more consistent, so your floors stay warm without cold spots.

If you're concerned about cost, you could also consider large-format porcelain slabs — they reduce grout lines, lower the chance of water infiltration, and look sleeker.

Porcelain with a polished finish can mimic the elegant look of marble while being far easier to maintain. You'll get the sophisticated appearance without the constant sealing required by natural stone. For a shower floor, I'd recommend a honed finish instead – it provides the refined aesthetic you're seeking while offering better slip resistance than polished surfaces.

The key is finding porcelain that captures marble's veining patterns without the maintenance burden. Many manufacturers now produce porcelain with realistic marble patterns that photograph beautifully but behave like high-performance engineering tiles.

A matte-finish porcelain tile with a surface rating of R10-R11, like the Daltile Slate Revo or the Emser Tile Corktown series, offers excellent slip resistance without the gritty, industrial look. Both lines are priced in the sweet spot between budget and premium, and they come in neutral tones that hide water spots and scuffs nicely.

Porcelain is the safer bet for a busy family bathroom—its density and low water absorption mean fewer stains and easier cleanup. A matte or honed finish gives better slip resistance than glossy, though it may show grout lines more. If you want a luxurious look without marble’s upkeep, choose porcelain that mimics marble patterns; they’re stain-resistant and handle high traffic.

Ceramic can still work, especially for walls, but pick a high-quality, low-absorption body rated for floors. Glazed finishes resist stains well, but watch for crazing (tiny cracks in the glaze) in older or cheaper tiles.

For the family bathroom, prioritize durability and easy maintenance. Porcelain with a matte finish offers the best balance of safety and low upkeep.

Porcelain is the clear winner for long-term durability and water resistance on a shower floor. Its dense, vitrified body absorbs less than 0.5% water, meaning it won’t soak up moisture the way cheaper ceramic does. That low absorption keeps the tile itself from cracking during freeze-thaw cycles and makes it very resistant to staining from hard water or beauty products.

Ceramic tiles are more porous, so they need a better sealant and tend to wear faster underfoot, especially when you’re dealing with daily moisture. Over time, porcelain’s structural strength keeps it looking new with minimal upkeep.

Cream of mushroom is definitely off the table; the lactose issue is a quick way to sour a family dinner. For gluten-free potato sides that still appeal to kids, you have two solid paths. First, toss baby Yukon Golds with olive oil, garlic, and a pinch of smoked paprika, then roast them until they’re crisp outside and fluffy inside—the paprika adds color and just enough flavor without spices that scream “healthy.” Second, if you want something softer for younger mouths, make dairy-free mashed potatoes using olive oil instead of butter and a splash of roasted garlic purée for richness; they’ll still be creamy and the garlic hides any unfamiliar taste. Both dishes blend right into the same meal and avoid any gluten cross-contamination.

Use a roux made with corn-free wheat-free starch like arrowroot or guar gum. Spoon the pan drippings into a saucepan, whisk in a teaspoon of the starch, and heat until glossy. Arrowroot gives a clear finish and works well with the lemon and herb flavors from the chicken.

Since you’re sticking to charcoal, make prep-ahead sides your saving grace. Salads like potato, pasta, and coleslaw all hold up well in the fridge and actually taste better after flavors meld overnight. For quick assembly, buy pre-chopped veggies and just mix in dressing at the last minute.

Watermelon cubes are another perfect option—slice a couple of melons, cube them, and keep them chilled on ice. They’re refreshing, kid-friendly, and require zero cooking.

For something warm but hands-off, try a slow cooker potato bake: layer frozen hash browns with cheddar, sour cream, and chives, set it low, and it’ll be ready when the grill finishes.

It’s pricier than cement-based grout, but it lasts decades without resealing. If budget is tight, urethane grout is a decent middle ground—water-resistant and flexible, though it still needs a quality sealer every few years. Skip sanded cement grout entirely; it cracks and stains in showers.

Epoxy grout is the gold standard for wet areas—it’s virtually waterproof, resists mold, and won’t discolor. A mid-range two-component system costs about $8–$12 per pound and lasts decades if installed properly. Avoid sanded cement grout in showers; it absorbs water and becomes a sponge for bacteria.

If you’re doing a DIY install, pre-mixed epoxy grout kits simplify the process, though they set faster so work in smaller sections. For a budget-conscious route, you can use a high-quality urethane grout, which is water-resistant and cheaper, though less abrasion-resistant than epoxy.

Roasted root vegetables are a fantastic gluten-free alternative. Toss diced carrots, potatoes, and parsnips in olive oil, salt, and pepper, then spread them around the chicken in the roasting pan so they cook together and absorb the flavorful drippings. It's hearty, simple, and keeps the meal cohesive without any gluten at all.

Absolutely — skip the cream, no problem. Here’s how to turn your chicken drippings into a rich, silky gluten-free gravy without any dairy:

1. **Get the pan right.** After you remove the chicken, pour the drippings into a measuring cup and let the fat rise. You’ll want to keep about one tablespoon of that fat for flavor; skim the rest off and discard if you’re watching calories.

2. **Thicken without flour.** Return the tablespoon of fat to the roasting pan. Sprinkle in one tablespoon of arrowroot powder (or 1½ teaspoons of cornstarch) and whisk until it’s a smooth paste. Both are naturally gluten-free and give you a glossy finish.

Marinated portobello caps work like mini steaks—brush them with garlic-herb oil, grill them cap-side down 8-10 minutes until tender. Corn on the cob is crowd-pleasing and safe; char it whole in foil with butter and salt, then finish with a light dusting of smoked paprika. If you want something with more body, try grilled halloumi skewers; they don’t melt, they just caramelize, and they’re dairy-safe for most (check labels for cross-contamination). A no-cook Mediterranean quinoa salad with cucumber, tomatoes, olives, and feta is sturdy enough to sit at room temp for hours and has zero shellfish. You can toss it the night before, refrigerate, and just fluff with a fork when you head out. Another easy option is a green bean–sugar snap peas salad dressed with a light lemon vinaigrette; the vegetables stay crisp even when chilled, and you can assemble everything in one large bowl. Both dishes travel well, feed a crowd, and look colorful on the table without needing a chafing dish or constant refreshing.

Skip the ribs and lean into lighter, portable sides. A chilled corn salad with lime and cilantro stays vibrant for hours and can be mixed the night before. Bring a batch of cucumber-tomato salad with a light vinaigrette; it’s refreshing and the dressings keep it from wilting. For a vegan-friendly staple, cook quinoa or couscous with herbs, then toss in diced bell peppers and red onion. Serve everything in shallow bowls so guests can stack plates easily.

Porcelain is the clear winner for underfloor heating. Because its structure is so dense, it conducts heat efficiently and evenly, so you get consistent warmth without cold spots. More importantly, its low porosity means thermal expansion and contraction are minimal, so the tiles are less likely to crack when the system cycles on and off. Ceramic, being more porous, can heat unevenly and is more prone to micro-cracking over repeated temperature changes.

A matte or honed porcelain finish can mimic the subtle movement of marble without the maintenance headaches—look for a matte glaze or a surface that’s lightly brushed to scatter light. Porcelain’s near-zero water absorption keeps it safe for shower floors, while matte glazes hide footprints better than high-gloss options. Some polished porcelain even carries a printed marble pattern; keep the finish matte instead of glossy to prevent slip hazards.

If you want a natural look without upkeep, consider a matte porcelain or honed ceramic that imitates stone veining. The key is choosing a finish that scatters light, not one that reflects it.

For a steamy bathroom floor, I'd recommend an epoxy grout or a high-quality polymer-modified cement grout with mold inhibitors. A 12×24 matte porcelain with a textured surface and a slip-resistance rating of R10 gives you solid traction without the quarry-tile look. Look for matte finishes with a “satin” or “soft-touch” coating—these slow water runoff and still feel comfortable underfoot.

For color, greys or warm beiges hide water spots better than stark whites, and subtle wood-look patterns add warmth without the maintenance headaches of real timber. Brands like Daltile’s “Carrara Matte” or MSI’s “Urban Ash” series hit mid-range price points and stock R10 ratings.

Look for a matte or lightly textured finish; these give natural traction without the slick surface that polished tiles create. A honed porcelain finish also hides small scratches better than high-gloss options.

Ceramic could work on walls for a budget break, but don’t install it on the floor. A single bottle of shampoo can seep into the pores and cause clouding or staining.

For color and pattern, lighter tones keep the room feeling bright and spacious, while darker shades hide dirt between cleanings. If you want the look of stone without the marble problems, many manufacturers make porcelain that perfectly mimics slate or limestone.

Cauliflower rice is a great option—toss it with some butter and the pan drippings for flavor. Quinoa works too, especially if you cook it in chicken broth and finish with chopped parsley. Both absorb the savory notes from the roast without any gluten.

You’ll want a cornstarch-thickened jus to stay both gluten-free and dairy-free. After roasting, pour the chicken pan drippings into a saucepan, skimming fat if you’d like, then whisk in a slurry of cornstarch and water until it’s smooth and glossy. Simmer two minutes so the starch cooks out; the result is a light gravy that coats the fork but won’t upset a sensitive stomach.

If you need more body without dairy or wheat, stir in a splash of vegetable broth or a teaspoon of miso paste for umami depth. Finish with a squeeze of lemon or a quick hit of fresh thyme to keep the flavor bright. This keeps the traditional roast-dinner feel while staying perfectly safe for everyone at the table.

Since Labs are food-motivated, keep training snacks under five calories each and reserve the bulk of her daily calories for her three regular meals. You can also let her “forage” by scattering kibble in puzzle toys, which burns mental energy and helps prevent overeating.

Rawhide is definitely off the table for a puppy like Ellie. For training treats, you want something soft, low-calorie, and quick to digest so she can stay focused on learning. Good options include small bits of cooked chicken breast, plain yogurt, or commercial soft training treats like Zuke’s Mini Naturals. You can also freeze small pieces of blueberries or carrots as crunchy rewards. Avoid anything with added sugars, artificial flavors, or hard textures that could damage her developing teeth.

If you prefer something slightly less touristy but still central, San Saba is a solid choice—small, residential, and within walking distance of the Pantheon.

By the way, if you’re into cafes that double as co-working spots when the sun’s out, look for places with outdoor terraces facing north—they stay cooler in July.
